# Timing report

A headless timing exercise, not a physics study. One fixed air-to-air engagement is flown once by itself, then 1000 times as a Monte Carlo sweep, and the measurement is wall-clock seconds.

All runs use the headless `bvr_batch` driver (no window, no rendering), back to back. Simulated time advances at a fixed 120 Hz regardless of wall clock.

**Machine:** AMD Ryzen 5 5600G with Radeon Graphics, 6 physical cores / 12 logical threads, Windows, Release build with link-time optimization (LTCG).  
**Measured:** 2026-11-02. Generated by `tools/analysis/timing_report.py`.

## The scenario

`tests/fixtures/scenarios/scenario_timing_5min.json`: a head-on intercept whose start is far enough out that the whole engagement runs about five minutes of simulated time.

| Element | Value |
|---|---|
| Geometry | Head-on, co-altitude, closing along the same line |
| Aircraft | Two JSBSim F-16s (full 6-DOF flight models) |
| Altitude / speed | 25,000 ft, 400 KTAS each (about 800 kt closure) |
| Initial separation | 525,000 ft (about 86 nmi) |
| Pursuer sensor | Airborne pulse-Doppler radar |
| Weapon | AIM-120 type, 12 m kill radius |

**Timeline** (seed 12345):

| Event | Sim time |
|---|---|
| RADAR_TRACK_ESTABLISHED | 176.0 s |
| LAUNCH_ZONE_ENTERED | 176.0 s |
| LAUNCH | 179.0 s |
| LOFT_END | 223.7 s |
| SEEKER_ACTIVE | 233.5 s |
| INTERCEPT | 274.1 s |

The run ends the instant the engagement resolves, at **274.1 s**. The real-time factor below divides by this engagement length.

## Test 1: single headless run

One run timed end to end (process start, JSON load, JSBSim load and trim of both aircraft, then the fixed-step loop to the intercept), five times back to back.

| Run | Wall time |
|---|---|
| 1 | 1.03 s |
| 2 | 1.00 s |
| 3 | 1.00 s |
| 4 | 1.01 s |
| 5 | 0.99 s |
| **Mean** | **1.01 s** |
| Real-time factor | 272x |

The cost is dominated by JSBSim: two full flight models stepped every tick.

## Test 2: 1000-run Monte Carlo

The same scenario, one run per seed (seeds 1 to 1000). Only the seed changes between runs; it reshuffles the radar's scan-to-scan RCS fluctuation, the datalink and seeker noise, and the warhead's Pk draw.

| Configuration | Wall time | Runs/s |
|---|---|---|
| 1 thread | 960.7 s (16 min 1 s) | 1.0 |
| 12 threads | 151.5 s (2 min 32 s) | 6.6 |
| Speedup | 6.3x | |

The win is doing many runs at once, not each run getting faster: per-run wall time rises under load as the workers contend for memory bandwidth. The ceiling is set by the 6 physical cores: the logical threads share them, and JSBSim is compute- and memory-bound, so hyper-threading adds little.

## Test 3: same results at any thread count

**Identical.** Every run's results row (every column but its own wall time) and every event row match between the 1-thread and the 12-thread sweep. Each run owns a random stream seeded from its own seed, so thread count changes only speed, never results.

## What the 1000 runs found

The outcomes are a byproduct, but they confirm the sweep did varied work.

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Runs launched | 1000 / 1000 |
| Hits (Pk) | 939 (0.939) |
| Miss distance | 0.00 m on 939 runs; median 0.00 m, largest 12236 m |
| Resolution time, mean (sd) | 267.0 s (11.7 s) |
| Resolution time, range | 215.4 to 299.7 s |
| Misses: self-destruct / other | 61 / 0 |

Pk is L(d)/L(0), 1 at 0 m ([REFERENCE 12.4](REFERENCE.md#124-probabilistic-lethality)), so a direct hit always kills.

## Summary

| Workload | Wall time |
|---|---|
| 1 run | 1.01 s |
| 1000 runs, 1 thread | 960.7 s (16 min 1 s) |
| 1000 runs, 12 threads | 151.5 s (2 min 32 s) |

*Method: `bvr_batch --spec <spec.json> --out <results.csv>`, `--jobs 1` and `--jobs 12`, via `python tools/analysis/timing_report.py`. Same Release binary throughout.*
